# PROJECT 1 — TCGA-BRCA \| Breast Invasive Carcinoma

With this project, we attempt to analyse RNA-seq gene expression data
from the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) BRCA cohort. The goal is to use
clinical and expression data for statistical analysis of the different
PAM50 subtypes and identifying patterns among other tasks.

**Reference:** The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (2012). Comprehensive
molecular portraits of human breast tumurs. *Nature*, 490, 61–70.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Setup — Load Libraries & Data

We load all required packages and the BRCA dataset provided as an
`.RData` file.

```{r}
load("BRCA_data.RData")
library(dplyr) 
library(ggplot2) 
library(pheatmap) 
library(caret)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
library(cluster)
library(pROC)
library(randomForest)
library(VennDiagram)
```

=======

# Part I - Gene Expression Analysis

## Step 1 — Data Structure Investigation

### How many samples and genes are in the expression matrix?

```{r}
# The dim() function returns the dimensions of your dataset: [1] Number of Rows (Genes), [2] Number of Columns. (Samples)

dim <- dim(brca_exp_clean)
df_dims <- data.frame("Genes" = dim[1], "Samples" = dim[2]) ; df_dims
```

### How many annotation columns are retained after cleaning to paper\_ columns?

We keep only the curated publication-level columns (those starting with
`paper_`) plus the `barcode` identifier. This filters out internal TCGA
processing columns that are not relevant for our analysis.

```{r}
# --- 1. Samples and Genes in the Expression Matrix ---

# indexes the annotations for the columns starting with paper, adding a barcode column for counting.
anot_paper <- brca_anot_clean[, c("barcode", grep("^paper_", names(brca_anot_clean), value = TRUE))]

dim <- dim(brca_anot_clean)
df_dims <- data.frame("Samples" = dim[1], "annotations" = dim[2]) ; df_dims
```

### What is the sample count per PAM50 subtype (paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)?

papter_BRCA-Subtype_PAM50 is our primary target variable. The PAM50
classifier assigns each tumour to one of five intrinsic subtypes: Basal,
Her2, LumA, LumB, and Normal-like.

```{r}
# Shows all PAM50 subtypes in a table. The "ifany" argument adds a column with the NA count if there are any NAs available.

subtype_counts <- table(anot_paper$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50, useNA = "ifany")

print("Sample count per PAM50 subtype:")
print(subtype_counts)
```

## Step 2 — Expression Distribution Analysis

## significant breast cancer genes from the paper (genes with the most consistent ):

The most variable genes mentioned in the paper are extracted and saved
for later analysis:

PIK3CA, PTEN, AKT1, TP53, GATA3, CDH1, RB1, MLL3, MAP3K1, CDKN1B, TBX3,
RUNX1, CBFB, AFF2, PIK3R1, PTPN22, PTPRD, NF1, SF3B1 and CCND3

```{r}
paper_top_genes <- c("PIK3CA", "PTEN", "AKT1", "TP53", "GATA3", "CDH1", "RB1", "MLL3", "MAP3K1", "CDKN1B", "TBX3", "RUNX1", "CBFB", "AFF2", "PIK3R1", "PTPN22", "PTPRD", "NF1", "SF3B1", "CCND3", "MDM2")

interesting_genes <- brca_exp_clean %>% filter(gene %in% paper_top_genes)
```

### Randomly select 10 genes and visualize their expression distributions across all samples.

For selecting random genes \`slice_sample\` is used. The expression is
visualized using a boxplot for readability and highlighting gene
variability across samples.

```{r}

set.seed(42) # For reproducibility
random_exp <- brca_exp_clean %>% slice_sample(n=10) # Subsetting the matrix to keep randomly selected genes
random_exp_long <- random_exp %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = where(is.numeric), 
               names_to = "Sample", 
               values_to = "Expression") # Reshaping data for ggplot2

ggplot(random_exp_long, aes(x = gene, y = Expression, fill = gene)) +
geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.size = 0.5) +  
  theme_minimal() +                                
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, face = "italic"), 
        legend.position = "none") +                
  labs(title = "Expression Distribution of 10 Randomly Selected Genes",
       x = "Gene",
       y = "Normalized Expression Level")


```

We see that even randomly selected genes exhibit a noticeable variation
among each other and among samples. For example YWHAZ has a
proportionally higher expression level than other genes and THSD4 is
highly variable across samples, seen from the bigger whiskers and 25%
and 75% quantile lines.

### Select the top 5 and bottom 5 most variable genes (by standard deviation); plot their distributions and compare.

```{r}
# Calculate gene variability (standard deviation)
# Calculate standard deviation for each gene (across all samples)
# Exclude the "gene" column, only use expression columns
gene_variability <- brca_exp_clean %>%
  mutate(gene_sd = apply(select(., -gene), 1, sd, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  select(gene, gene_sd) %>%
  arrange(desc(gene_sd))

# Top 5 most variable
top5_variable <- head(gene_variability, 5)
cat("Top 5 Most Variable Genes:\n")
print(top5_variable)

top_20_most_variable <- head(gene_variability, 20)

# checking if the interesting genes are found in the top variable genes 
top_20_most_variable %>% filter(gene %in% interesting_genes) # nope

# Bottom 5 least variable
bottom5_variable <- tail(gene_variability, 5)
cat("\nBottom 5 Least Variable Genes:\n")
print(bottom5_variable)

# Combine gene lists
variable_genes <- c(top5_variable$gene, bottom5_variable$gene)

# Extract and transform data
var_exp <- brca_exp_clean %>%
  filter(gene %in% variable_genes) %>%
  pivot_longer(-gene, names_to = "Sample", values_to = "Expression") %>%
  mutate(Variability = ifelse(gene %in% top5_variable$gene, "High", "Low"))

# Plot comparison
ggplot(var_exp, aes(x = reorder(gene, Expression, FUN = median), 
                    y = Expression, 
                    fill = Variability)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("High" = "red", "Low" = "blue")) +
  labs(title = "Expression Distribution: High vs Low Variability Genes",
       subtitle = "Top 5 and Bottom 5 genes by standard deviation",
       x = "Gene",
       y = "Normalized Expression (log2)",
       fill = "Variability") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

```

We calculated the sd values of each gene across all samples using the
`apply`command.

The 5 most variable genes are all clinically significant in the context
of breast cancer as they are all markers and checkpoints, meaning their
upregulation and downregulation mark transitions in the state of the
disease (Lacroix et al. 2006).

The least variable genes are, as expected, housekeeping genes. For
example, HNRNPs are conserved across species and contribute to nucleic
acid metabolism (Geuens et al. 2016).

## Step 3 — Correlation Analysis

## Prerequisite — Sample Alignment

Before running any analysis that combines the expression matrix with the
annotation file, we must ensure that both objects contain **exactly the
same samples in the same order**. Mismatches would silently corrupt all
downstream results.

```{r}
#First set the column "gene" as rownames 
brca_exp_clean_ctr <- brca_exp_clean %>%
  column_to_rownames("gene")
```

```{r}
# TRUE = Reihenfolge stimmt bereits überein, kein Alignment nötig
all(colnames(brca_exp_clean_ctr) == anot_paper$barcode)
```

Because the the result says "TRUE" we don't need to correct the
alignment. The order and dimensions are aligned. Else we would have to
write the following alignment command with `intersect`:

```{r}
#Find samples that appear in BOTH the expression matrix "brca_exp_clean" AND the significant annotation file "anot_paper"
common_samples <- intersect(colnames(brca_exp_clean_ctr), anot_paper$barcode)

#Subset both objects to the shared samples (same order in both)
expr_clean <- brca_exp_clean_ctr[ , common_samples]
anot_clean <- anot_paper[match(common_samples, anot_paper$barcode), ]
```

### Compute pairwise Pearson correlations across all samples using the full gene set.

We compute **pairwise Pearson correlations** between all samples using
the full gene set. The resulting $N×N$ correlation matrix is visualized
as a heatmap. Samples are annotated by PAM50 subtype so we can judge
whether the correlation structure reflects known biology.

The Pearson correlation measures linear co-expression: two samples with
similar expression profiles across all genes will have a correlation
close to 1. If PAM50 subtypes are transcriptionally distinct, we expect
to see high within-subtype correlations forming visible blocks along the
diagonal.

```{r}
#calculate Pearson-correlation matrix between all samples. 
#convert to numeric matrix (required by c())
expr_mat <- as.matrix(brca_exp_clean_ctr)


#cor() applied column-wise computes correlation betweent samples. Each column = one sample's expression profile across all genes
cor_mat <- cor(expr_mat, method = "pearson")
```

```{r}
#unwichtig -> gibt mir die dimensions der correlation matrix was logischerweise 1099x1099 ist da das die sample zahl ist
# gibt auch die value range
cat("Correlation matrix dimensions:", dim(cor_mat)[1], "x", dim(cor_mat)[2], "\n")
cat("Corr Value range: [", round(min(cor_mat), 3), ",", round(max(cor_mat), 3), "]\n")
```

### Visualize as a correlation heatmap. What structure do you observe? Are there sub- blocks?

```{r}
#colors for PAM50-Subtpyes
pam50_colors <- c(
  Basal = "red",
  Her2 = "orange",
  LumA = "blue",
  LumB = "green",
  Normal = "purple"
)

# annotation for heatmap
sample_annotation <- data.frame(
  PAM50 = anot_clean$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50,
  row.names = anot_clean$barcode
  )

# plot heatmap
pheatmap(
  cor_mat,
  annotation_col = sample_annotation,
  annotation_row = sample_annotation,
  annotation_colors = list(PAM50 = pam50_colors),
  show_rownames = FALSE,
  show_colnames = FALSE,
  color = colorRampPalette(c("navy","white","red"))(100),
  main = "Pairwise Pearson Correlation",
  treeheight_row = 30,
  treeheight_col = 30
)
```

### Interpret: does the correlation structure correspond to PAM50 subtypes?

The heatmap shows a clear **block-diagonal structure** that aligns
closely with the PAM50 subtype annotation:

-   **Basal** samples form the most isolated, highest-contrast block —
    their expression programme is fundamentally different from all other
    subtypes. This is consistent with the TCGA paper, which found
    basal-like tumours to have the most distinct multi-platform
    signature.
-   **LumA and LumB** share a broad luminal block with high mutual
    correlation, reflecting their common ER⁺ biology. The differences
    between them are more quantitative (e.g., proliferation rate) than
    qualitative.
-   **Her2** sits between the luminal and basal blocks, showing moderate
    correlation with both.
-   **Normal**-like samples are the most heterogeneous.

The existence of these sub-blocks confirms that PAM50 subtypes represent
genuinely distinct transcriptional states, not arbitrary labels.

Furthermore, we can also plot the correlations of top genes as a heatmap
to get an overview:

```{r}

# Correlation between top varying genes 

gene_vars <- apply(brca_exp_clean_ctr, 1, var)

# 2. Extract the names of the top 500 most variable genes
top_genes <- names(sort(gene_vars, decreasing = TRUE)[1:50])

# 3. Subset the original matrix, transpose, and re-calculate correlation
expr_mat_subset <- as.matrix(brca_exp_clean_ctr[top_genes, ])
cor_t_mat_small <- cor(t(expr_mat_subset), method = "pearson")

# Find out which genes have the highest correlation


cor_matrix_clean <- cor_t_mat_small
diag(cor_matrix_clean) <- NA # take out the diagonal

# 2. Set correlation threshold (e.g., absolute correlation > 0.8)
threshold <- 0.8

# 3. Identify genes that have at least one correlation above the threshold
# This checks row by row to see if any value exceeds the threshold
highly_corr_logical <- rowSums(abs(cor_matrix_clean) > threshold, na.rm = TRUE) > 0

# 4. Save the names to a vector
highly_correlated_genes <- rownames(cor_matrix_clean)[highly_corr_logical]
# plot heatmap
pheatmap(
  cor_matrix_clean,
  show_rownames = T,
  show_colnames = T,
  color = colorRampPalette(c("blue","white","red"))(100),
  main = "Pairwise Pearson Correlation",
  treeheight_row = 30,
  treeheight_col = 30,
  fontsize = 5
)

cat("highest correlating genes:\n",highly_correlated_genes)
```

The shown `highly_correlated_genes` are genes (or groups of genes) that
co-express or genes that are upregulated as the others are
downregulated. Both negative and positive correlations are seen here
since the absoloute value of the correlation values has been taken.

Interestingly, three of these genes are also seen in the most highly
variable genes shown in **part 1** (SCGB2A2, SCGB1D2, TFF1). These genes
belong to a group of genes that are upregulated and co-expressed in LumA
and LumB subtypes (Zafrakas et a. 2006). They are correlated since they
belong to the same group and are most likely variable between the LumA
and LumB patients and the other subtypes.

## Step 4 — Hierarchical Clustering

### Cluster samples using hclust.

Here we tried both the silhouette method and the elbow method for
finding the optimal `k` value for clustering. Both of these methods work
by measuring euclidean distances of data points, hence we use . The
elbow method did not yield any readable results as it lacked the
essential "elbow". We therefore do not present its results, as to not
overfill the output with plots.

```{r clustering-and-silhouette}
# 1. DATA PREPARATION & DISTANCE CALCULATION

# Transpose matrix so patients are rows, then calculate Euclidean distance
exp_t <- t(brca_exp_clean_ctr)
D <- dist(exp_t)

# 2. HIERARCHICAL CLUSTERING
hc_result <- hclust(D, method = "ward.D2")
```

```{r}
# Find out average silhouette scores with 2-8 centriods
k_values <- 2:8
sil_avg <- sapply(k_values, function(k) {
  km <- kmeans(x = exp_t, centers = k, nstart = 10)
  s <- silhouette(km$cluster, D)
  mean(s[, 3])
}) # k=2 is optimal

tibble(k = k_values, avg_silhouette = sil_avg)

# Plot silhouette for the best k (expected: k = 2)
km_best <- kmeans(x = exp_t, centers = 2, nstart = 10)
s_best <- silhouette(km_best$cluster, D)
plot(s_best, col = "blue", border = NA,
     main = paste("Silhouette Plot for K-means (k =", best_k, ")"))
```

The average silhouette score was not desirable, but the highest was
achieved with two centroids. This problem with the clustering is because
of the data not being heterogeneous enough and there not being enough
data points generally. Furthermore, biological overlap between LumA and
LumB amoung others, also prevents optimal clustering.

## Cut the dendrogram to obtain k clusters (choose k; justify your choice).

Here we use `cuttree` to well... you can guess. The handy `rect_hclust`
is subsequently used to visualize the clusters.

```{r}
# Cut the tree at k = 2
hc_clusters <- cutree(hc_result, k = 2)

plot(hc_result,
     labels = FALSE,
     main = "Hierarchical clustering of BRCA samples",
     xlab = "Samples",
     ylab = "Height")
rect.hclust(hc_result, k = 2, border = "red")

# check cluster sizes for k=2
table(hc_clusters)
```

### Compare cluster membership with PAM50 subtypes.

```{r}
# --- Comparison for k = 2 ---
cluster_df <- data.frame(barcode = names(hc_clusters), 
                         hc_cluster = hc_clusters)

comparison_df <- merge(cluster_df, anot_paper, by = "barcode")

comparison_table <- table(Cluster = comparison_df$hc_cluster, 
                          PAM50 = comparison_df$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)


# --- Comparison for k = 5 ---
cluster_df_5 <- data.frame(barcode = names(hc_clusters_5), 
                           hc_cluster = hc_clusters_5)

comparison_df_5 <- merge(cluster_df_5, anot_paper, by = "barcode")
comparison_table_5 <- table(Cluster = comparison_df_5$hc_cluster, 
                            PAM50 = comparison_df_5$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)

print("Cluster Membership vs. PAM50 Subtypes (k=2):")
print(comparison_table)

subtype_counts
```

The clustering comparison shows that the Basal-like subtype is quite
different than all the other subtypes, placing it in its own cluster and
while other clusters are comfortable where they are, Normal type also
has a noticable number of samples in the basal-type cluster.

## Step 5 — PCA Visualization

### Plot PC1 vs. PC2 and PC1 vs. PC3, colored by PAM50 subtype and by hierarchical cluster

```{r PCA}
# feeding the transposed exp dataset into prcomp
pca_result <- exp_t %>% # samples as rows
  prcomp(center = TRUE, scale = FALSE) # use data centering,   

# Creates a dataframe and combines it with the annotation
pca_with_annot <- as.data.frame(pca_result$x) %>%
  merge(anot_paper, by.x = 0, by.y = "barcode") 
  # by.x = 0 uses the PCA rownames, by.y = "barcode" uses the annotation column

ggplot(pca_with_annot, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Basal" = "red", "Her2" = "blue", 
                                "LumA" = "darkgreen", "LumB" = "lightgreen", 
                                "Normal" = "grey"))
ggplot(pca_with_annot, aes(x = PC1, y = PC3, color = paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Basal" = "red", "Her2" = "blue", 
                                "LumA" = "darkgreen", "LumB" = "lightgreen", 
                                "Normal" = "grey"))

```

### Report the variance explained by the first three PCs. What distinguishes the subtypes?

PC1 captures the most variance in the dataset and mainly distinguishes
between Basal and Luminal BRCA tumors. This indicates that the biggest
biological difference in breast cancer is between hormone-receptor
negative (Basal) and hormone-receptor positive (Luminal) tumors.

Even though the first plot shows an overlap between Luminal A and
Luminal B tumors, PC2 does seem to distinguish them slightly.
Furthermore it also seems to distinguish between HER2- and normal-like
subtypes. PC3 on the other hand doesnt seem to distinguish between PAM50
subtypes, which indicates that it may distinguish between secondary
biological factors, such as Tumor microenviornment

One can also see that the differences and the variation between the
first and the second plot being much less in the second one. This is
because of the lack of information in PC3 compared to PC2.

## Step 6 — Differential Expression

We use a **Wilcoxon rank-sum test\* in a** one-vs-rest\* design to find
marker genes for each PAM50 subtype. For every gene we test if it shows
a significant difference in expression in one subtype compared to all
other subtypes combined.

A Wilcoxon test is used because it is **non-parametric**, which means it
does not assume a normal distrubution. This is appropriate for RNA-seq
date that can be skewed. Also it is robust against outliers.

After testing, we apply a **Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction** (BH) to
police the false discovery rate across the many tests performed. Also we
report the **top 20 genes per subtype** sorted by adjusted p value.

### Use a Wilcoxon rank-sum test (one-vs-rest) to identify marker genes for each PAM50 subtype.

```{r}
# verctor with subtype names for use in loop 
subtypes <- c("Basal", "Her2", "LumA", "LumB", "Normal")

#define function that takes a subtype name as input and tests all genes for that subtype
wilcoxon_one_vs_rest <- function(subtype){
  is_subtype <- anot_clean$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50 == subtype #one: is true if the sample belongs to the subtype and false if not
  is_rest <- !is_subtype #rest: opposite of is_subtype: true for all other samples
  
  #rownames gives us gene names, lapply circles through all gene names and executes following code. The result is a list with one entry per gene. The following code extracts expression values of subtype samples (expr_subtype) and rest-samples (expr_rest), as.numeric ensures those are numeric
  
  results <- lapply(rownames(expr_clean), function(gene) {
    expr_subtype <- as.numeric(expr_clean[gene, is_subtype])
    expr_rest <- as.numeric(expr_clean[gene, is_rest])
    
#executes Wilcoxon test, exact = FALSE means that an approximation is used, exact calculation is too slow
    
    wt <- wilcox.test(expr_subtype, expr_rest, exact = FALSE)
    
#log2 Fold Change measures how big the difference is: the mean of the subtype samples is devided by the mean of the rest of the samples. 1e-6 ensures that there is no division with 0. Meaning of the results: lfc = 1 -> expression twice as high, lfc = -1 -> expression is half, lfc = 0 -> no difference in expression
    
    lfc <- log2((mean(expr_subtype) + 1e-6) / (mean(expr_rest) + 1e-6)) 
    
#For every gene the result is saved in a data frame with 4 column
    
    data.frame(gene = gene, subtype = subtype,
               p_value = wt$p.value, log2FC = lfc)
  })
  
#results are now a list if 2994 small data frames (one per gene). rbind glues data frames together. do.call uses rbind on all elemts on the list. This results in a singular data frame with 2994 rows for this subtype
  
do.call(rbind, results)
}

#lapply tales test_subtype for each of the 5 subtypes, the result is a list of 5 data frames with each having 2994 rows. do.call glues them together again resulting in a dataframe of 14970 rows 

de_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(subtypes, wilcoxon_one_vs_rest))

```

### Apply FDR correction (BH). Report the top 20 genes per subtype by adjusted p-value and log2 fold-change.

We have executed 14970 tests. That leads to many random false-positives.
p.adjust(method = "BH") corrects p-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg
method. group_by(subtype) ensures a seperate correction by subtype and
mutate adds the corrected p-values as a new column p_adj

```{r}
de_results <- de_results %>%
  group_by(subtype) %>%
  mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH")) %>% # Benjamin Hochberg FDR adjustment (rank based)
  ungroup()
```

Top report the top 20 genes per subtype by adjusted p-value and log2
fold-change we first sort by smalles p_adj (most significant first) and
if p_adj valuea are equal then sort by highest absolute log2FC
(strongest effect first). slice_head(n=20) only keeps the top 20 genes
per subtype. abs() is used because we want both up- and downregulated
genes.

```{r}
top20 <- de_results %>% 
  group_by(subtype) %>% 
  arrange(p_adj, desc(abs(log2FC))) %>% # adds expression data
  slice_head(n=20) %>% 
  ungroup() #undos the group_by(subtype)

## seeing if the interesting genes in the paper are in the top 20 DEGs

top20 %>% filter(gene %in% interesting_genes) # nope 
top20 %>% filter(gene %in% gene_variability)
```

```{r}
# heatmap with the adjusted p-values. change p_adj to log2fc for the expression.
heatmap_data <- top20 %>%
  select(gene, subtype, log2FC) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = subtype, values_from = log2FC)

# Convert to a true numeric matrix with gene names as row names
heatmap_matrix <- as.matrix(heatmap_data[, -1])
rownames(heatmap_matrix) <- heatmap_data$gene

# Replace any missing values (NAs) with 0 if necessary
heatmap_matrix[is.na(heatmap_matrix)] <- 0

max_abs <- max(abs(heatmap_matrix), na.rm = TRUE)
breaks <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 51)

color_palette <- colorRampPalette(c("navy", "white", "red3"))(50)

pheatmap(
  t(heatmap_matrix),
  color = color_palette,
  breaks = breaks,
  cluster_rows = TRUE,
  cluster_cols = TRUE,
  scale = "none",
  border_color = "black",
  display_numbers = FALSE,
  fontsize = 10,
  fontsize_row = 8,
  fontsize_col = 5,
  main = "Differential Gene Expression per Subtype (Log2FC)"
)


```

With this plot we see that the differential expression of the highest
variable genes is very similar in most genes, but does differ in some
genes. We must note here, that for the sake of visibility the scale is
set to highest/lowest expression to be at 2/-2 since most variations lie
in this range but most notably, the KRT16 gene (last gene of LumB) has
the value -10 but is shown to be shown as the same color as the other
genes. A z-score normalization would have been a possible soloution to
this.

We see here that almost all of the DEGs are differentially expressed in
their own subtype. The most notable exception here is FOXC1, which is
upregulated in Basal but downregulated in LumB.

### Generate an annotated heatmap (rows = top DEGs, columns = samples, annotation bars = PAM50 subtype and pathologic stage).

We take the samples from the expression matrix and line them up with the
DEGs and perform a z-score-normalization, so that saturated genes are
normalized and subtype baselines are established.

```{r}
top_gene_names <- unique(top20$gene) #generates all unique gene names of the top 20 of all subtypes (5*20 = 100 genes). 
#
heatmap_mat     <- as.matrix(expr_clean[top_gene_names,])
heatmap_z       <- t(scale(t(heatmap_mat))) #Scale() usually normalizes by row, but by column is needed thats why doubled transpontation is needed. After normalization 0 means average expression, +2 means two units of standard deviations above average. This is important so the colours of the heatmap show relative expression and not the absolute values. Otherwise genes with a high overall expression would dominate the color profile.

#annotation table for the heatmap columns. The rownames need to be the barxodes so pheatmap knows which annotation belongs to which sample

col_annotation <- data.frame(
  pam50 = anot_clean$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50,
  Stage = anot_clean$paper_pathologic_stage,
  row.names = anot_clean$barcode
)

#sorting of the heatmap columns and the annotation in the same order -> all basal samples together, then Her2 and so forth. With that the subtype blocks become more apparent
col_order <- order(col_annotation$pam50)
heatmap_z_sorted <- heatmap_z[, col_order]
col_annot_sorted <- col_annotation[col_order, , drop = FALSE]
stage_levels <- levels(factor(col_annotation$Stage))
stage_colors <- setNames(
  c("Stage_I" = "#1b9e77",
    "Stage_II" = "#7570b3",
    "Stage_III" = "#d95f02",
    "Stage_IV" = "#e31a1c")[stage_levels],
  stage_levels
)
pheatmap(
  heatmap_z_sorted,
  annotation_col = col_annot_sorted,
  annotation_colors = list(Stage = stage_colors),
  show_rownames = TRUE, #show gene names
  show_colnames = FALSE,
  cluster_cols = FALSE, #dont cluster columns again since they are already sorted
  cluster_rows = TRUE, #cluster genes using expression pattern
  color = colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))(100),
  main = "Top DEGs per PAM50 Subtype (Z-scored expression)",
  fontsize_row = 3
)
```

Looking at the overview, there is no obvious difference seen between
various stages and high/low expression of genes, although we would
expect this. There is however, a difference in expression seen amoung
subtypes as seen before, when we looked at the highest varying genes.

To investigate the difference of expression in the stages, we cut the
DEG dataset by subtype and limited the sample number to see if distinict
patterns start to show up.

```{r}

# two-sample heatmap for a chosen subtype
subtype_choice <- "LumB"
subtype_gene_names <- top20 %>%
  filter(subtype == subtype_choice) %>%
  pull(gene) %>%
  unique()

subtype_samples <- rownames(col_annot_sorted)[col_annot_sorted$pam50 == subtype_choice]
set.seed(42)
selected_samples <- if (length(subtype_samples) >= 2) {
  sample(subtype_samples, 40)
} else {
  subtype_samples
}

two_sample_mat <- as.matrix(expr_clean[subtype_gene_names, selected_samples, drop = FALSE])
two_sample_z <- t(scale(t(two_sample_mat)))
two_sample_annot <- col_annot_sorted[selected_samples, , drop = FALSE]

pheatmap(
  two_sample_z,
  annotation_col = two_sample_annot,
  annotation_colors = list(Stage = stage_colors),
  show_rownames = TRUE,
  show_colnames = F,
  cluster_cols = FALSE,
  cluster_rows = TRUE,
  color = colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))(100),
  main = paste("Top 20", subtype_choice, "DEGs (2 samples)"),
  fontsize_row = 6,
  fontsize_col = 8
)

```

But no, at least visually, there is no difference seen. Even when single
columns stand out, there are other columns reporting the contrary, so
one cannot reliably say that there is a real correlation.

Alternatively, a t-test or a variant of it could have also been used to
find statistically significant DEGs accross stages in each subtype.

We can also look at the top z_score normalized genes:

```{r}
top10_by_z <- heatmap_z %>%
  abs() %>%
  apply(1, max, na.rm = TRUE) %>%
  sort(decreasing = TRUE) %>%
  head(10)

top10_by_z
```

We now see among the top 10 scaled DEGs, some classic cancer markers.
These all, in some way or the other, help the tumor grow (TCGN, 2012).

## Step 7 — Prediction Models

### Binary task — tumor vs. normal: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, k-NN. Report confusion matrices and AUC-ROC.

#### Logistic regression

We do not have any data for "normal" patients. The next closest thing to
normal is the normal subtype amoung the PAM50 subtypes so we take this
subtype and compare it against the rest. Here we do not expect good
models since the normal subtype is not that different than the other
subtypes according to the PCA. A better comparison would have been
between one of the Luminal types and Basal.

For binary analysis of the data, we need to annotate the subtypes
properly, so that we have either a "normal" or a "tumor". For this, we
can use `dplyr`. Afterwards, the data is cleaned and prepared for
machine learning. All categorical data, with the exceptiopn of
`PAM50subtypes`, are made into numeric and NAs are omitted.
`PAM50subtypes` is also saved as a factor with two levels: `tumor` and
`Normal`Additionally, the top 30 genes with the most sd (which are
believed to be highly variable) are aligned with the samples to have
more parameters for the training.

```{r}
# Function to remove columns with lots of NAs (more than half of the entries).
#Used later on in the script.

#find the columns with more than "p" NAs (0.5 for 50%) and removes them using indexing
nacol_rm <- function(df,p){
too_many_nas <- colSums(is.na(df)) > round(nrow(df)*p)
bad_column_names <- colnames(df)[too_many_nas]
df <- df[, !too_many_nas]
}
```

```{r}

# Coverstion of subtypes into binary:
normal <- anot_paper %>% filter(paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50 == "Normal") 
tumor <- anot_paper %>% filter(!paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50 == "Normal") 
tumor$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50 <- "tumor"
binary_data <- rbind(normal,tumor)

# Adding gene expression data of the genes with the highest variance. While ignoring highly correlated genes as to not diminish the effect of single parameters and increase error.
sig_genes <- head(gene_variability, 30) %>% 
  filter(!gene==highly_correlated_genes)

gene_indexes <- as.vector(rownames(column_to_rownames(sig_genes,"gene"))) 

exp_cols <- as.data.frame(exp_t[,gene_indexes]) %>% rownames_to_column("barcode")


binary_data <- binary_data %>% 
  inner_join(exp_cols, by = "barcode") %>% 
    column_to_rownames("barcode") %>% # Rownames to cols
 mutate(across(-paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50, ~ as.numeric(as.character(.)))) %>%
    nacol_rm(p=0.5) %>% 
  na.omit()

binary_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50 <- factor(binary_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50, levels=c("tumor","Normal"))

```

We use `caret` to create 70/30 training and testing datasets.

```{r}

# -----------------Using caret to create the test and training data------------
set.seed(161)
trainIndex <- createDataPartition(binary_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50,
                                  p = 0.7, list = FALSE)

train_data <- binary_data[trainIndex, ]
test_data  <- binary_data[-trainIndex, ]

```

Starting with a logistic regression model, we use the `glm` function
from `stats` while using the binomial family to specify the type as a
logistic regression. We check the final results using the `summary`
function. For generating a cross-tabulation table, first the prediction
is made on the test data. Subsequently, the result of the prediction is
in probabilities and needs to be turned back into the factor values.
After this step is cross-tabulation table can be generated.

```{r Logistic regression}

# Creating the model using the glm function from the stats library while using the binomial family to specify the type as a logistic regression. 

model_logit <- glm(paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50 ~ ., data = train_data, family = "binomial")

summary(model_logit)

# Predict
prob_logit <- predict(model_logit, test_data, type = "response")
pred_logit <- ifelse(prob_logit > 0.5, "Normal", "tumor")
pred_logit <- factor(pred_logit, levels = levels(test_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50))

confusionMatrix(pred_logit, test_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)

```

Here the model obviously lazily gusses all entries as tumor since the
training data only had 28 patients with normal type PAM50 subtype. It
interestingly does not use the clinical data for training as much as the
expression data. That is except for days to birth, initial diagnosis age
and date to last follow up, which makes sense since these could affect
gene expression and subsequently subtype specification. However since
the samples are all breast cancer patients and we are differentiating
between subtypes, this would hardly differ. Especially since Basal is
the most age dependant subtypes are luminal and basal and these are both
in the tumor category (Jenkins, 2014).

The genes that were mostly used were also probably top correlated
between the normal subtype samples.

```{r}
# testblock
train_control <- trainControl(
  method = "repeatedcv",
  number = 5,
  repeats = 3,
  classProbs = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = multiClassSummary, # Handles multi-class data evaluation
  sampling = "down"                    # Fixes class imbalance automatically
)

# Fit a Random Forest or Penalized Multinomial Model
optimized_model <- train(
  paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50 ~ ., 
  data = train_data, 
  method = "rf", # or "glmnet" for lasso/elastic net
  metric = "Balanced_Accuracy",
  trControl = train_control
)
```

#### K-Nearest Neighbor:

Using the `train()` function with `method=kNN` we can use this method,
that leveraged eucleadian distances for binary classification. Here we
manually specify the number of neighbors with `tuneGrid` to exclude too
low or too high k values. We also use a cross validation with 5 samples
using `trainControl`. The necessary preprocessing was also done to
calculate the correct distances.

```{r}
# Train k-NN

model_knn <- train(
  paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50 ~ .,
  data = train_data,
  method = "knn",
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(k = seq(3, 21, by = 2)),  # Wider range for ~200 samples
  trControl = trainControl(
    method = "cv", 
    number = 5, 
    classProbs = TRUE,
    summaryFunction = twoClassSummary  # Binary-specific metrics
  ),
  preProcess = c("center", "scale")  # CRITICAL for kNN
)

# Predict directly on test_data (no need for test_norm)
pred_knn <- predict(model_knn, test_data)
confusionMatrix(pred_knn, test_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)
```

The same pattern of the logistic regression results is seen in the kNN
method as well, with kappa somehow dropping into the minus, meaning
there were less than one correct prediction. This agains has to do with
the skewed data.

```{r}
# Plot k selection

plot(model_knn)

model_knn$bestTune[,"k"] # optimal k
```

We see that the optimal k is 13, meaning 13 neighbors for each data
point.

#### Random forest

For this section we could have either used `train` with `method="rf"` or
just used the `randomForest` library, which we did the exercises for in
the course. We went for the library. Here we also use backward selection
with `step` to exclude parameters based on their correlation with each
other (high correlation=bad).

```{r}
# Fit the random forest model
# Using caret to create the test and training data

model_rf <- randomForest(paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50 ~ ., data = train_data, importance = TRUE, ntree = 500, step="backward") 

# Predict
pred_rf <- predict(model_rf, test_data)
confusionMatrix(pred_rf, test_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)
```

```{r}
# Finding out Important features
imp_params <- varImp(model_rf, main = "Feature Importance")

# saving the values and the genes in a dataframe for possible comparison with other models
rf_varimp <- tibble("important parameters"=rownames(imp_params[23:33, ]), 
       imp_params[23:33, 1])

# plotting out the 1o most important parameters
varImpPlot(model_rf, main = "Feature Importance", n.var = 10)



```

The feature importance plot shows that the most important feature is the
AGR3 gene followed by a TFF1, etc. Interestingly, these genes are among
the highly correlated genes by Pearsons correlation. This alignment
makes biological sense, as the non-linear decision trees within the
Random Forest independently isolate these tightly co-expressed luminal
markers as the most robust features for purifying and segregating the
tumor subtypes.

### Method comparison

```{r}
truth_bin <- test_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50

# Simple overall metrics (Accuracy, Precision, Recall, Weighted F1)
simple_metrics <- function(pred, truth) {
  lvls <- union(levels(as.factor(truth)), levels(as.factor(pred)))
  truth <- factor(truth, levels = lvls)
  pred  <- factor(pred, levels = lvls)

  tab <- table(Prediction = pred, Reference = truth)
  tp <- diag(tab)
  fp <- rowSums(tab) - tp
  fn <- colSums(tab) - tp
  support <- colSums(tab)

  precision <- tp / (tp + fp)
  recall    <- tp / (tp + fn)
  f1        <- 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)

  precision[is.nan(precision)] <- NA_real_
  recall[is.nan(recall)]       <- NA_real_
  f1[is.nan(f1)]               <- NA_real_

  tibble(
    Accuracy = sum(tp) / sum(tab),
    Precision = sum(precision * support, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(support),
    Recall = sum(recall * support, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(support),
    WeightedF1 = sum(f1 * support, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(support)
  )
}

models_bin <- list(
  "Logistic regression" = pred_logit,
  "k-NN" = pred_knn,
  "Random forest" = pred_rf
)

metric_tbl <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(models_bin), function(m) {
    simple_metrics(models_bin[[m]], truth_bin) %>% mutate(Model = m)
  })
)

metric_tbl
```

The high scores here are because of the skewed data. Since the high
majority of the data was comprised of the "tumor" subtype (all except
normal), most guesses were right.

### ROC curves for binary classification:

```{r}

truth <- droplevels(test_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)

# Logistic: prob_logit is already numeric from glm
p_logit <- prob_logit  # check: this is P(class == "Normal") if levels are c("tumor","Normal")

# Random forest probs
p_rf <- predict(model_rf, newdata = test_data, type = "prob")[, "tumor"]
p_knn <- predict(model_knn, newdata = test_data, type = "prob")[, "tumor"]


roc_logit <- roc(truth, p_logit, levels = c("tumor", "Normal"))
roc_rf    <- roc(truth, p_rf,    levels = c("tumor", "Normal"))
roc_knn   <- roc(truth, p_knn, levels = c("tumor", "Normal"))

plot(roc_logit, col="blue", main="ROC Curves", lwd=2)
lines(roc_rf, col="green", lwd=2)
lines(roc_knn, col="red", lwd=2)
legend("bottomright", legend=c("Logistic","Random Forest","k-NN"),
       col=c("blue","green","red"), lwd=2)
```

```{r}
rocs <- c(auc(roc_logit),auc(roc_knn),auc(roc_rf))
tibble(models=c("Logistic Regression", "k-Nearest Neighbors", "Random Forest"),
       AUC=rocs)

```

### Binary class summary:

Binary classification doesn't work at all since the normal subtype is
not easily found among the other PAM50 subtypes. This makes the model
strongly biased towards a positive guess, which results in the high
sensitivity and low specificity scores throughout. However, since the
lazy guesses are "technically" mostly right, the AUCs and other model
testing data looks good.\
------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Multiclass task — predict PAM50 subtype: Random Forest, Multinomial Logistic Regression, k-NN.

#### Random Forest:

For the multiclass classification we need to make another dataframe
without the binary classification and also again add the expression
dataset. We also need a new training index.

```{r}
set.seed(161)

sig_genes <- head(gene_variability, 30) %>% 
  filter(!gene==highly_correlated_genes)

gene_indexes <- as.vector(rownames(column_to_rownames(sig_genes,"gene"))) 

exp_cols <- as.data.frame(exp_t[,gene_indexes]) %>% rownames_to_column("barcode")


multi_data <- brca_anot_clean %>% 
  inner_join(exp_cols, by = "barcode") %>% 
    column_to_rownames("barcode") %>% # Rownames to cols
 mutate(across(-paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50, ~ as.numeric(as.character(.)))) %>%
    nacol_rm(p=0.5) %>% 
  na.omit()

multi_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50 <- factor(multi_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50, levels = c(unique(multi_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)))
trainIndex <- createDataPartition(multi_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50,
                                  p = 0.7, list = FALSE)

train_data <- multi_data[trainIndex, ]
test_data  <- multi_data[-trainIndex, ]
```

```{r}
model_rf <- randomForest(paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50 ~ ., data = train_data, importance = TRUE, ntree = 500, step="backward")

varImpPlot(model_rf, main = "Feature Importance")

# Predict
pred_rf <- predict(model_rf, test_data)
confusionMatrix(pred_rf, test_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)

```

Right away, we can see that the multi-class test fits out data better
since the model is not only reported to be better than the null model (P
\< 0.05), but it has a much lower NIR (0.53 instead of 0.96) meaning its
taking a lot of fewer guesses and the specificity and sensitivity of the
test also returns good values, especially at subtypes: Her2 and Basal
but also LumA.

#### kNN - Multi class:

here we use the same command but with `multiClassSummary` as
`summaryFunction`.

```{r}

model_knn <- train(
  paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50 ~ .,
  data = train_data,
  method = "knn",
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(k = seq(3, 31, by = 2)),
  trControl = trainControl(
    method = "cv", 
    number = 5, 
    classProbs = TRUE,
    summaryFunction = multiClassSummary  # Use for multiclass, not default
  ),
  preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
  metric = "Balanced_Accuracy"  # Better than Accuracy for imbalanced multiclass
)

# Predict
pred_knn <- predict(model_knn, test_data)
confusionMatrix(pred_knn, test_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)

```

#### Multinomial logistic regression:

this is the equivalent to the logistic regression. it calculates the
log-odds for each category, taking one class as a base-line. Then it
converts these odds into probabilities, on which it uses the Maximum
Likelihood Estimation algorithm to calculate parameters.

```{r}
model_multinom <- train(paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50 ~ ., 
                        data = train_data, 
                        method = "multinom",
                        trace = FALSE,
                        trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5))

# Predict
pred_multinom <- predict(model_multinom, test_data)
confusionMatrix(pred_multinom, test_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)
```

For the comparison of the roc curves, we use `droplevels` to take true
labels for subseting subtypes and then we use pROC to get the rocs out
of predictions. We then use a loop to plot each roc line.

```{r}

truth <- droplevels(test_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)

prob_multinom <- predict(model_multinom, newdata = test_data, type = "prob")
prob_rf       <- predict(model_rf,       newdata = test_data, type = "prob")
prob_knn      <- predict(model_knn,      newdata = test_data, type = "prob")

# Multiclass AUC (macro-averaged)
roc_multinom <- multiclass.roc(truth, prob_multinom)
roc_rf       <- multiclass.roc(truth, prob_rf)
roc_knn      <- multiclass.roc(truth, prob_knn)

classes <- levels(truth)
roc_list <- lapply(classes, function(cls) {
  roc(response = truth == cls,
            predictor = prob_rf[, cls], # change prob for different model
            levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
            quiet = TRUE)
})

plot(roc_list[[1]], col = 1, lwd = 2, main = "Random Forest: one-vs-rest ROC")
if (length(roc_list) > 1) {
  for (i in 2:length(roc_list)) lines(roc_list[[i]], col = i, lwd = 2)
}
legend("bottomright", legend = classes, col = seq_along(classes), lwd = 2)
```

In our case, unlike the binary classification, multi-class ROCs cannot
show the summary of the models performance, but rather the performance
between subtypes. Here we see that Basal has the best performance and
normal has the worst so lets take a look at them more closely:

For viewing all models' performances, we can subset by subtype:

for calculating AUCs, `proc` is used again.

```{r}
tibble(models=c("Multinom", "k-Nearest Neighbors", "Random Forest"),
```

```{r}
rocs <- c(
  auc(roc_multinom),
  auc(roc_knn),
  auc(roc_rf)
)

tibble(
  models = c("Multinomial Logistic", "k-Nearest Neighbors", "Random Forest"),
  AUC = rocs
)

```

### For each model, report: accuracy, F1, per-class precision/recall.

```{r}
# Multiclass metrics per model (standalone)
metrics_from_preds_mc <- function(pred, truth) {
  lvls <- union(levels(as.factor(truth)), levels(as.factor(pred)))
  truth <- factor(truth, levels = lvls)
  pred  <- factor(pred, levels = lvls)

  tab <- table(Prediction = pred, Reference = truth)
  tp <- diag(tab)
  fp <- rowSums(tab) - tp
  fn <- colSums(tab) - tp
  support <- colSums(tab)

  precision <- tp / (tp + fp)
  recall    <- tp / (tp + fn)
  f1        <- 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)

  precision[is.nan(precision)] <- NA_real_
  recall[is.nan(recall)]       <- NA_real_
  f1[is.nan(f1)]               <- NA_real_

  per_class <- tibble(
    Class     = colnames(tab),
    Support   = as.integer(support),
    Precision = as.numeric(precision),
    Recall    = as.numeric(recall),
    F1        = as.numeric(f1)
  )

  overall <- tibble(
    Accuracy   = sum(tp) / sum(tab),
    MacroF1    = mean(f1, na.rm = TRUE),
    WeightedF1 = sum(f1 * support, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(support)
  )

  list(confusion = tab, overall = overall, per_class = per_class)
}

truth_mc <- droplevels(test_data$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)

models_mc <- list(
  "Multi Log" = pred_multinom,
  "k-NN"                = pred_knn,
  "RF forest"       = pred_rf
)

eval_mc <- lapply(models_mc, metrics_from_preds_mc, truth = truth_mc)

overall_tbl <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(eval_mc), function(name) {
    eval_mc[[name]]$overall %>% mutate(Model = name)
  })
)

per_class_tbl <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(eval_mc), function(name) {
    eval_mc[[name]]$per_class %>% mutate(Model = name)
  })
)

overall_tbl
per_class_tbl
```

The comparison of the models shows how the variation of the different
PAM50 subtype features affects the model's classification performance.
Overall we see good values for Basal and LumA, with Her2 also returning
good values in multinom and RF but not kNN (probably because its
datapoints landed near others and there needed to be more datapoints
generally). The Normal subtype, again, suffers from the small number of
datapoints and lack of noticeable transcriptional difference with the
other subtypes.

```{r}
  fill = c("#4daf4a", "#377eb8"),
  alpha = 0.6,
  cex = 1.1,
  cat.cex = 1,
  cat.pos = c(-20, 20),
  cat.dist = c(0.05, 0.05)
)

grid.newpage()
grid.draw(venn_plot)


venn.plot <- draw.pairwise.venn(
  area1 = length(deg_set),
  area2 = length(top_rf_genes),
  cross.area = length(overlap_genes),
  category = c("DEG top20", "RF top20"),
  fill = c("#4daf4a", "#377eb8"),
  alpha = c(0.6, 0.6),
  cex = 1.0,
  cat.cex = 0.9,
  cat.pos = c(-20, 20)
)
```

The analysis shows that the two overlapping genes between DEGs and RF
are AGR3 and TFF1. These genes also happen to be differentially
expressed luminal like breast cancers, marking less aggressive responses
when highly expressed (Kvamme, 2026 ; Obacz 2015). Using the expression
values of these genes the model could successfully differentiate between
these subtypes and the others. Furthermore, this minimal overlap
demonstrates that while the DEG pipeline relies strictly on individual
gene expression variability, the Random Forest model leverages complex,
non-linear interactions among a more diverse ensemble of features to
achieve classification.

The fact that only these two genes are selected by the model has to do
with the high number of luminal like samples in the dataset. \# Part II
— Clinical Data Analysis

## Step C — Clinical Feature Classification

### Predict a binary or multi-class clinical outcome using clinical variables only (no expression data).

### Define the outcome variable and apply appropriate encoding.

We define vital status as outcome variable (predicting whether a patient
is 'Alive' or 'Dead' based on their clinical profile)

### Select a small set of meaningful features (age, stage, grade, subtype, etc.) and handle missing values by imputation or exclusion.

```{r}
# We select features, drop missing values, and encode categorical data as factors
ml_data <- anot_paper %>%
  select(paper_vital_status, paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis, 
         paper_pathologic_stage, paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(
    Target = factor(paper_vital_status, levels = c("Alive", "Dead")),
    Age = paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis,
    Stage = as.factor(paper_pathologic_stage),
    PAM50 = as.factor(paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)
  ) %>%
  select(-paper_vital_status, -paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis, 
         -paper_pathologic_stage, -paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)

```

### Train/test split (70/30 or 5-fold CV). Fit: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, k-NN.

```{r}
## TRAIN / TEST SPLIT
set.seed(42) # For reproducible splits

trainIndex <- createDataPartition(ml_data$Target, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
train_data <- ml_data[trainIndex, ]
test_data  <- ml_data[-trainIndex, ]

## MODEL TRAINING (with 5-fold CV)

cv_ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5, classProbs = TRUE, summaryFunction = twoClassSummary, savePredictions = "final")

lr_model <- train(Target ~ ., data = train_data, method = "glm", family = "binomial",
                  trControl = cv_ctrl, metric = "ROC")
rf_model <- train(Target ~ ., data = train_data, method = "rf", 
                  trControl = cv_ctrl, metric = "ROC")
# k-NN relies on distance, so we MUST center and scale the Age variable automatically
knn_model <- train(Target ~ ., data = train_data, method = "knn", 
                   trControl = cv_ctrl, metric = "ROC", preProcess = c("center", "scale"))

print(lr_model)
print(rf_model)
print(knn_model)
```

### Report confusion matrices, accuracy, sensitivity/specificity, and AUC-ROC for each model.

```{r}

set.seed(42) 
## PREDICTIONS & CONFUSION MATRICES

# Logistic Regression
pred_lr_class <- predict(lr_model, newdata = test_data)
pred_rf_class <- predict(rf_model, newdata = test_data)
pred_knn_class <- predict(knn_model, newdata = test_data)

# Print Confusion Matrices (Includes Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity)
cat("\n--- Logistic Regression Confusion Matrix ---\n")
confusionMatrix(pred_lr_class, test_data$Target)

cat("\n--- Random Forest Confusion Matrix ---\n")
confusionMatrix(pred_rf_class, test_data$Target)

cat("\n--- k-NN Confusion Matrix ---\n")
confusionMatrix(pred_knn_class, test_data$Target)
              
```

```{r}

set.seed(42) 
# AUC-ROC AND PLOTTING

# Get predicted probabilities for the test set (using "Alive" as the event of interest)
prob_lr  <- predict(lr_model, newdata = test_data, type = "prob")
prob_rf  <- predict(rf_model, newdata = test_data, type = "prob")
prob_knn <- predict(knn_model, newdata = test_data, type = "prob")

# Compute ROC
roc_logit <- roc(response = test_data$Target, predictor = prob_lr$Alive, levels = c("Alive", "Dead"))
roc_rf    <- roc(response = test_data$Target, predictor = prob_rf$Alive, levels = c("Alive", "Dead"))
roc_knn   <- roc(response = test_data$Target, predictor = prob_knn$Alive, levels = c("Alive", "Dead"))

# Print AUC values
cat("\n--- AUC Values ---\n")
cat("Logistic Regression AUC:", roc_logit$auc, "\n")
cat("Random Forest AUC:", roc_rf$auc, "\n")
cat("k-NN AUC:", roc_knn$auc, "\n")

# Plot ROC curves
plot(roc_logit, col = "blue", main = "ROC Curves (Test Set)", lwd = 2)
lines(roc_rf, col = "green", lwd = 2)
lines(roc_knn, col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Logistic Regression", "Random Forest", "k-NN"),
       col = c("blue", "green", "red"), lwd = 2)
```

### Identify the most predictive clinical features: variable importance from RF, and coefficients from Logistic Regression. Note that k-NN does not provide native feature importance.

```{r}
set.seed(42) 
# Random Forest Variable Importance Plot
rf_importance <- varImp(rf_model, scale = FALSE)
plot(rf_importance, main = "Random Forest Feature Importance")

# Logistic Regression Coefficients / Importance
# Using summary() to see raw coefficients and p-values
cat("\n--- Logistic Regression Coefficients ---\n")
summary(lr_model$finalModel)

# Optional: Plot Logistic Regression Variable Importance
lr_importance <- varImp(lr_model, scale = FALSE)
plot(lr_importance, main = "Logistic Regression Feature Importance")
```

## Step D — Integrative Analysis (Expression + Clinical)

### Correlate top DEGs from Part I with continuous clinical variables (e.g., age) using Spearman's rho.

```{r}
stepD_genes <- unique(top20$gene)
stepD_genes <- intersect(stepD_genes, rownames(expr_clean))

stepD_samples <- intersect(colnames(expr_clean), anot_clean$barcode)
stepD_expr <- as.data.frame(t(expr_clean[stepD_genes, stepD_samples, drop = FALSE]))
stepD_expr$barcode <- rownames(stepD_expr)

stepD_clin <- anot_clean %>%
  select(
    barcode,
    paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis,
    paper_pathologic_stage,
    paper_vital_status,
    paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50
  ) %>%
  filter(barcode %in% stepD_samples)

stepD_df <- inner_join(stepD_clin, stepD_expr, by = "barcode")

age_corr_tbl <- lapply(stepD_genes, function(gene) {
  x <- stepD_df[[gene]]
  y <- stepD_df$paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis
  ok <- !is.na(x) & !is.na(y)
  if (sum(ok) < 3) {
    return(tibble(gene = gene, rho = NA_real_, p_value = NA_real_))
  }
  ct <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(x[ok], y[ok], method = "spearman"))
  tibble(gene = gene, rho = unname(ct$estimate), p_value = ct$p.value)
}) %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  arrange(p_value)

age_corr_tbl %>% slice_head(n = 10)
```

### Test whether top DEGs differ significantly across clinical stages.

```{r}
stage_diff_tbl <- lapply(stepD_genes, function(gene) {
  x <- stepD_df[[gene]]
  grp <- stepD_df$paper_pathologic_stage
  ok <- !is.na(x) & !is.na(grp)
  if (length(unique(grp[ok])) < 2) {
    return(tibble(gene = gene, p_value = NA_real_))
  }
  kt <- suppressWarnings(kruskal.test(x[ok] ~ grp[ok]))
  tibble(gene = gene, p_value = kt$p.value)
}) %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  arrange(p_value)

stage_diff_tbl %>% slice_head(n = 10)
```

### Build a multimodal classifier: combine top expression features (from Step 7 / RF importance) with key clinical features. Does adding clinical data improve performance?

```{r}
stepD_top_expr <- age_corr_tbl %>%
  filter(!is.na(p_value)) %>%
  arrange(p_value) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  pull(gene)

stepD_model_df <- stepD_df %>%
  select(
    barcode,
    paper_vital_status,
    paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis,
    paper_pathologic_stage,
    paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50,
    all_of(stepD_top_expr)
  ) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(
    Target = factor(paper_vital_status, levels = c("Alive", "Dead")),
    Age = paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis,
    Stage = as.factor(paper_pathologic_stage),
    PAM50 = as.factor(paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)
  ) %>%
  select(Target, Age, Stage, PAM50, all_of(stepD_top_expr))

set.seed(42)
stepD_idx <- createDataPartition(stepD_model_df$Target, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
stepD_train <- stepD_model_df[stepD_idx, ]
stepD_test  <- stepD_model_df[-stepD_idx, ]

stepD_ctrl <- trainControl(
  method = "cv",
  number = 5,
  classProbs = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary
)

rf_clin <- train(
  Target ~ Age + Stage + PAM50,
  data = stepD_train,
  method = "rf",
  trControl = stepD_ctrl,
  metric = "ROC"
)

rf_multi <- train(
  Target ~ .,
  data = stepD_train,
  method = "rf",
  trControl = stepD_ctrl,
  metric = "ROC"
)

prob_clin <- predict(rf_clin, newdata = stepD_test, type = "prob")[, "Alive"]
prob_multi <- predict(rf_multi, newdata = stepD_test, type = "prob")[, "Alive"]

roc_clin <- roc(stepD_test$Target, prob_clin, levels = c("Alive", "Dead"))
roc_multi <- roc(stepD_test$Target, prob_multi, levels = c("Alive", "Dead"))

tibble(
  Model = c("Clinical only", "Expression + clinical"),
  AUC = c(auc(roc_clin), auc(roc_multi))
)
```

### Visualize: boxplots of top expression features stratified by clinical subgroups; annotated heatmap with both molecular and clinical annotation bars.

```{r}
plot_genes <- head(stepD_top_expr, 4)

box_df <- stepD_df %>%
  select(paper_pathologic_stage, paper_vital_status, all_of(plot_genes)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(plot_genes), names_to = "Gene", values_to = "Expression")

ggplot(box_df, aes(x = paper_pathologic_stage, y = Expression, fill = paper_pathologic_stage)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ Gene, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Top DEG expression by clinical stage",
    x = "Pathologic stage",
    y = "Expression"
  )

heat_genes <- head(stepD_top_expr, 10)
heat_mat <- as.matrix(expr_clean[heat_genes, stepD_samples, drop = FALSE])
storage.mode(heat_mat) <- "numeric"
heat_z <- t(scale(t(heat_mat)))

heat_annot <- stepD_clin %>%
  filter(barcode %in% colnames(heat_z)) %>%
  select(barcode, paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50, paper_pathologic_stage, paper_vital_status) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.factor)) %>%
  as.data.frame()
rownames(heat_annot) <- heat_annot$barcode
heat_annot$barcode <- NULL
heat_annot <- heat_annot[colnames(heat_z), , drop = FALSE]

pheatmap(
  heat_z,
  annotation_col = heat_annot,
  show_colnames = FALSE,
  fontsize_row = 6,
  main = "Top expression features with clinical annotations"
)
```
